utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. Good morning, everyone. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams -- no, not all the accused are here. Mr. Beara is not here. I understand he is sick. Do we have a waiver?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I got a call last night, late, and he asked that he be allowed to rest today and the Detention Unit informed me he would have so sign a waiver today not to obstruct the trial, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, we don't have it. So do we have your go-ahead at least as counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, you do. And it should be here. They told me this morning that he had signed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. That makes a difference, if you've been told that he has signed it already. So Mr. Ostojic and Mr. Mrkic are not here. Ms. Condon is not here. What's happened to Ms. Condon?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Condon will be with us from next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And Mr. Ostojic and Mr. Mrkic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, Mr. Ostojic will be with us next week also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And Mr. Mrkic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Mrkic has resigned from our team. He's no longer with the Beara Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Vanderpuye. I don't know if there is anyone else behind the column. No. Did I miss anyone else? Mr. Sarapa is here. Mr. Petrusic is here. Forgive me but the column is in the way and I have to move various directions to see who is not hiding but who happens to be behind the column. All right. Mr. McCloskey, I know that -- I'm referring you specifically to the latest motion, confidential motion, filed by the Nikolic team. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for pointing that out, Mr. Josse. All right. There seems to be no other preliminaries apart from the topic, the subject matter, that some of you have intimated would like to address the Chamber upon. So we move directly to that issue. Who wishes to address the Trial Chamber first? Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, honourable Judges, the Defence has certain concerns concerning the motion of the Prosecution. These concerns are of administrative nature and in my opinion should not be submitted before this Chamber. Unfortunately, I'm forced once again to bring to the notice of the Chamber our financial problems that we could face if this joinder occurs. In paragraph 2 of his motion, the Prosecutor says that joinder would not cause financial prejudice to the accused and that it would protect the limited resources of the parties in the proceedings before the Chamber and the Prosecutor asserts that the rights of the accused will be fully observed. The paragraph applies both to the accused Tolimir and the other accused. In paragraphs 35 and another paragraph of the motion, the Prosecutor claims that a postponement of five to six months is advisable to prepare for this knew joined case. All the accused are covered by the motion, including the accused Tolimir. Without prejudice to any position the Defence might take in the future regarding the joinder, I have to raise before this Chamber the issue of payments for the Defence if the joinder occurs, and we are all aware that postponement will occur necessarily if the joinder is approved. The Prosecutor correctly notes in his motion that the adjournment in the proceedings should be taken advantage of for purposes of preparation, on both sides. However, the Defence is now facing the possibility that they will not be paid. In other words, that their remuneration would be considerably reduced during that adjournment. It needs not even be said that we will not be able to work if we are not paid, we will not be able to prepare defence, and our clients will in that period be deprived of defence. The right to defence is one of the basic rights that is protected by various conventions, including the statute of this Tribunal. One of the integral parts of the right to defence is provision of resources to the accused for purposes of preparing a defence. In keeping with that, if, during the adjournment we are not paid, that will clearly have an effect and will be a grave violation of Article 21 of the statute, whereas the joinder would clearly be against the interests of our clients and would again be a violation of Article 21 of the statute and will be a denial of the right to defence. I regret very much that my position on the joinder has to be linked with an administrative issue, namely payment for Defence. However, I cannot take my position on the Prosecutor's motion before I know what kind of resources will be at the disposal of the Defence during the adjournment. We have already addressed the registrar very soon after receiving the motion of the Prosecutor, and we received a very worrisome answer. They say that we should not be concerned because the motion has nothing to do with legal assistance but reality is very different. We do not know at this moment whether we would be able to work in the next five or six months or not. Therefore, I urge you, Your Honours, to instruct the Registry to give us an answer, a positive answer, assuring us that we will have sufficient resources during the adjournment, resources that are simply a required minimum for an effective defence. Now I have to raise another issue, namely the issue of deadlines. In paragraph 26 of his motion, the Prosecutor asks that all time starts to count from the moment the accused Tolimir is assigned a counsel. I want to know whether the same applies to our six accused here. I urge the Chamber to take a decision setting deadlines for the seven accused here and that time starts to count from the decision of the Registry. I apologise again to the Chamber because I was forced to raise administrative problems in the courtroom where they have no place. However, I emphasise once again that if adjournment occurs, we have to use it in the best possible way for purposes of defence of our accused because many new documents will come to light and we have to work on them. We also have to have the necessary resources for that in order to be able to respond in the best possible manner to the motion of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau-Ivanovic, if I can ask you a question because I'm not well aware of the situation. My understanding is that as for resources, the Defence counsel are paid in lump-sum basis. My question is whether that lump sum -- the amount of lump-sum payment depends upon the length of time, the length of time of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The amount of -- we have at our disposal depends on the duration of the trial and that's why precisely my colleague, Mr. Ostojic, has asked for the Prosecution case to be prolonged because for the moment we are paid until 15th of August, but when we received the motion of the Prosecutor, I raised the question before the Registry whether and what will be done in case of adjournment, whether this adjournment will be treated as part of the trial or as a break but they were not in a position to tell us whether this will count as the Prosecution case or a purely an adjournment, and for the moment, our situation is one of complete uncertainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think this basically raises two issues. One is not really related to the subject matter that we are discussing, and usually I was telling Judge Kwon as Presiding Judge I am called upon to sign a document periodically indicating the estimated length of trial because I know that the lump sum covers a certain period of time and I think you can rely on us taking care of that because there is no way this trial can finish in August, so that much you don't need to worry about. On the other hand, the matter that you raise, whether the adjournment, the four or five months, would be considered as a break or as part of the trial, in other words an ongoing part of trial, is a very valid point that we've taken note of. Can I ask you who you consulted from the registrar's office, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We contacted immediately after the motion was filed, Mr. Martin Petrov and we also wrote a letter to Mr. John Hocking, Deputy Registrar, and we received yesterday Mr. Hocking's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what does it say?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Basically the letter says that the-- their decision will depends on the decision of the Trial Chamber. I believe they referred to the decision on joinder, and they say that our position must not be linked to the decision on joinder because it's a financial matter, but in fact our situation is completely different. We have to know what our financial situation will be before we know what we think about the joinder. In fact, we have to know whether this adjournment will benefit or be prejudicial to our clients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And when you approached Mr. Petrov did you get a reply from him, a formal response, in writing or orally?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, but I believe the reply of Mr. Hocking also covers Mr. Petrov because the letter was copied to the latter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And were these representations made by you only or together with others present at the time? Other Defence counsel, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The letter to the Registry was written in the name of six Defence teams. I do not know if the seventh Defence team is in agreement with what we presented yesterday but I believe they agreed with the letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which is the seventh Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's us, Your Honour. There is a very small difference in nuance between us and some of my learned friends. We clearly are concerned about the matter but we would approach it in a slightly different way but that is certainly not something that we need to air in front of the Trial Chamber at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Anyone else wishes to address the Trial Chamber from the Defence teams first? Mr. Meek? I'll give you the floor very soon, Mr. McCloskey. Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour, upon your question to Ms. Fauveau. John Ostojic did talk personally with Mr. Petrov last week and asked that question, and the answer that I'm aware of was that there are directives on that and that's all he would say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have an indication of which directives he was referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, it's the legal aid directive, Your Honour, talking about if there is a stop in the trial, they can basically have the right to cut us down to 40 per cent of what the lump sum might be for lead counsel and co-counsel. That would be the maximum amount they could but that's what they are referring to. I don't have the exact rule right now but I could get it for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Anyone else? Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, briefly, Mr. President, I normally stay out of these issues. However, since the Tolimir arrest I have been in touch with Defence counsel on all these issues and I do share their concern about finances. I spoke briefly to Martin Petrov and I found his attitude to be positive. It's just such an unusual situation, the possibility of joinder, that I think he's looking to us and to you especially to give him some guidance on what this may involve. I told him that "break" would not be a proper word for this, that the actual work would increase so the intensity of trial would not. So I think he's looking to the Court and to everyone to see if -- what is warranted and my view is that there will be more work, and that I will be getting as many, if not more, e-mails late at night from Defence, and motions and preparation. So to give him an idea that this is not a break in the sense of that we may normally think of a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. If we grant -- if we grant joinder because obviously we haven't -- we are not even in a position to start discussing it this deeply because we haven't got any responses either from the Defence teams here or for that matter from the Tolimir -- from Tolimir or his Defence team, when he gets one, the situation as I understand it, if there is -- if there will be a four-to-five month hiatus, whoever is appearing for Tolimir or will be appearing for Tolimir certainly will be paid because for that lawyer, that would not be a stoppage in any case, and the same argument then supposedly cannot be used in relation to these ladies and gentlemen over here. So that immediately brings, highlights a discrepancy. But in any case, I don't think we are in a position to discuss with you any further on this. We need to consider it. There are these issues that need to be decided without delay. Number 1 is for Tolimir, there is the problem of running of the time limits for filing of the response, and that depends on the decisions that will be taken as to whether he will defend himself or whether he will be assisted by counsel. That's problem number 1, and we are not privy to any developments in that sector as yet. The other thing is that if I understand Madam Fauveau correctly, while the reason for suspending the time limits applicable to Tolimir would not be applicable to you, strictly speaking, still you would like the time limit to be suspended until the registrar has communicated to you his decision on matters of finance, and in that case, the time limit will start running from the date of that decision. Did I read you well, Madam Fauveau, or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Do you wish to -- yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I just would like to add quickly on this issue, the reason being that as soon as the motion for joinder was filed, we have started consulting of course with our respective clients as to whether we should oppose or whether we should be in favour of the joinder. The problem is we are not in a position to advise our clients in a proper manner because we don't know what we will be able to do during this period. We know what the Prosecution will do. Mr. McCloskey has made that very clear, that he will continue working full blast ahead and we would like to be able to be in a position to advise our clients. We have offices, we have staff, our staff has indicated to us that they will be leaving if they are not paid. Then that means we have to start all over again. We have to shut down our offices, bring those back home and then start again four months from now. If that is the case, we need to be able to discuss this with our client to see what we can do during this period and that is the case why we just want, once we know what we can do, then we are in a position to respond to the Prosecution's joinder motion. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fully understood, Mr. Bourgon. Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I just turn to the other issue and that's the issue of time for our response? I thought my learned friend Madam Fauveau's submission was that our time should run from the time of General Tolimir. In other words, when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I didn't understand her that way. That's why I made sure that I had understood her well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In a sentence, that's the submission I make on behalf of General Gvero, that our time should run from the time of General Tolimir. It would cause no administrative inconvenience bearing in mind General Tolimir won't file his response until such time as the Trial Chamber says he has to. We should be in the same position, I submit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, can I just clarify? You say you're seeking the same time limits that are imposed with respect to Mr. Tolimir; is that correct? Not that you want it to run from the time Mr. Tolimir files a response.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The same time limit as General Tolimir, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Point taken. Any further submissions, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. There were four issues that we wanted to address the Trial Chamber with this morning. Mrs. Fauveau took care of the first two issues. I would like to address the third issue and my colleague Mr. Haynes will be addressing the Trial Chamber, with your leave, with respect to the your fourth issue. With your leave, Mr. President, I will now move on to this issue and once again I address here the Trial Chamber on behalf of six of the accused in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you specify who?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, counsel representing the accused Gvero have a different position, a slightly different position, which they may be able to articulate themselves after I've done my own argument, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Our submission at this time is that, in light of the Prosecution's motion for joinder, of the -- joinder of the proceeding against Zdravko Tolimir to this case, we are of the view that it would be both inappropriate and counter-productive to proceed with the testimony of any further Prosecution witness until the Prosecution motion has been decided upon. In short, Mr. President, we believe that this is the case both for legal, as well as practical, reasons. My colleagues representing the accused Pandurevic will later address you specifically with the situation applicable to Mr. Zdravko Tolimir, the newly arrested person but for now what I'd like to say is that considering the fact that Mr. Tolimir is presently in The Hague, that he is available for this trial, although he has not yet instructed counsel, and the fact that the Prosecution have clearly indicated their intention to join him to this case, it's only a matter of time before we have a decision whether he will or not be joined. We believe that proceeding in his absence would amount to some kind of a trial in absentia, given the fact that he has a right to be present at any trials involving himself, and there is a motion out there which says that that it is -- this is the intention of the Prosecution. Moreover, Mr. President, many of the witnesses scheduled between now and 28 June, and I say 28 June because this is the date referred to by the Prosecution in the motion, for stopping this trial if Mr. Tolimir is joined, and many of these witnesses are related to the acts and conduct of Zdravko Tolimir, or are of such importance to this case that the accused, who for all intents and purposes will be the most senior in this case if he's joined, will -- should be present to hear the testimony of these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon are you speaking on behalf of Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm not speaking -- no, Judge. I'm speaking about the accused in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please concentrate on your client's position.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will, I will, Judge. For now let me just add that we believe that it is not for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sorry, thank you. Mr. President, we believe for the time being that it is not for the Prosecution to decide or suggest which witnesses would be recalled in the event Mr. Tolimir is joined to this case or not. We believe that it would be counter-productive to proceed with any further witness at this time only to have them recalled at a later time if and when, of course, Mr. Tolimir decides to call these witnesses back. We believe that should the Trial Chamber take the view that we should continue hearing witnesses for the purpose of saving time, which we could understand, that the Trial Chamber is interested in moving along with this trial, and so are we on this side of the courtroom, we are interested in moving along with the proceedings. However, we feel that if Mr. Tolimir is joined to this case, this may have an impact on the cross-examination that we could be doing once he is in the courtroom because as the most senior accused, his position he takes will have an impact on the cross-examination that we may lead with any given witnesses. And for this reason, we believe that if the Trial Chamber should take the view that we are to proceed with witnesses until we have a joinder decision, then in such a case that we only hear examination-in-chief and that we keep cross-examination for once we know whether Mr. Tolimir is joined or not to this case. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It might be easier if I respond to Mr. Bourgon perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. I think it would be more appropriate for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I fundamentally agree with most of what Mr. Bourgon is saying, that - and I think you can see that from the motion - going forward with the possibility, strong possibility of joinder creates the problems for a joined trial. The reason we suggested the 28th of June or July 2nd was a balancing between the odds frankly of a joinder and the time saving that we would have by putting on witnesses that we didn't think would have a significant effect on General Tolimir. So as I think the Court has known, we have put off several witnesses that were former accused and some other witnesses to do that. And so we have tried to balance the interests because of the uncertainty of the situation. As we state, and as you know, the health of the General Tolimir is an issue, and though we were -- we all saw him and heard him and we have some more positive feelings on that, though it's just feelings at this point, we need doctors' reports, we need to hear from Mr. Tolimir again. So another thing we didn't have when we filed the motion was the view of the Defence, while we had talked to them briefly. The view I'm getting, aside from the financial view, and let me make it clear: I don't think finances can be an issue here. There is no doubt they need to be paid what they have been getting paid because the work is going to be more, so finances cannot be an issue. I think the Registry just needs to hear from all of us on that. But now I have heard from them after they've had a chance to talk to their lawyer, and unless something has changed, they appear to be unanimous on -- in the joinder. And this is an extremely significant and important situation. You can imagine all of us being unanimous on something as important as the arrest and so I think as we look at the odds and the chances of joinder and we compare it to some of the issues we pointed out in our motion, it looks like joinder is becoming ever more a reality, though that's your decision, I'm not going to begin to say what your decision is, but with the Defence being unanimous, the Prosecution being unanimous and, yes, we need to hear from General Tolimir but I don't need to remind anyone, General Tolimir has been on the run for a long time and, yes, he has rights to be heard on this but I think that needs to be part of any evaluation when he's looking at the trial of his colleagues and the co-accused. So I tend to agree with what much of what counsel has said. We do have two witnesses that are here this week and I think at a minimum we should handle them and get them done but after that, I am open to the Court, to counsel, and in this unusual situation, to see what we think is best because going on does create problems. None of us want to waste one hour in this courtroom or a day on the chance that something might be joined but I think those chances are getting high enough that the balance is getting closer to declaring a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The submission I'm about to make -- I think Mr. Josse wants to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I just make a brief submission in relation to that last matter because I think Mr. Haynes is moving on to a different manner. Your Honour, we, too, broadly speaking agree with everything that's being said. On balance, on behalf of General Gvero, we would rather make as much progress as the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution think is possible in the circumstances. Not putting too fine a point on it, our client is not getting any younger and he would like to see the day that this trial might actually end, and if there is some real prospects of a little bit of progress being made, we on balance would rather that progress is made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That applies not only for your client but also -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I mean I hope he won't mind me saying, sir, I think he's the oldest person in this room now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Josse. Congratulations, General Gvero. Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The submission I have to make is frankly not an easy one but it's been alluded to. And I'm conscious in making it of the fact that I'm making submissions that substantially concern someone who is not here and does not presently have the benefit of the representation of counsel. And I'm equally conscious of the fact that this Chamber as presently constituted may consider itself to have only a limited ability to make directions of the sort which I submit are at least desirable, though I acknowledge that the Tribunal is one body and I was comforted to note that the initial appearance of General Tolimir was presided over by a member of this Trial Chamber who was very familiar with the facts of this case. I'm also conscious of the fact that the submissions I make may seem to strike at the very hearts of the rights of an accused person. However, I represent, in common with all seven of my colleagues in this case, a man who surrendered himself to the custody of the Tribunal and has, through his own conduct and the conduct of his lawyers, done everything he can to assist in the expedient trial of this case. Before we even come to the question of the resolution of the Prosecution's motion, there remains the question of how that can ever come to pass. General Tolimir must, of course, be heard on that issue but when, where and how is a rather more intricate question. The Prosecution frankly are to be commended for their request at paragraph 36 of their motion, which, in case you don't have it immediately to hand, is the request that all time limits be subject to General Tolimir's instruction of counsel. It is, on their part, a full and proper acknowledgement of the rights of the accused to counsel and I dare say General Tolimir is very grateful that time does not start to run for him until he has been assigned counsel. However, on behalf of my client, I'm bound to question the wisdom of according him quite so much freedom to take his time to choose. There may be reasons to expect he will instruct a lawyer in the not-too-distant future or rumours or so on and so forth. However, the only concrete evidence we have about his willingness to cooperate with the judicial process of this Tribunal is his absence of choice of the last few years. Whatever, if granted, the request at paragraph 36, I submit, builds into the process of the resolution of this motion uncertainty and an element of uncontrollability. The range of possibilities in terms of how time might slip in this initial stage of proceedings is almost limitless. Of course, it's no part of my submission that General Tolimir should be punished for being at large by having his right to counsel qualified or removed. And of course, many things can, for legitimate reasons, go wrong. However, nor should he, in my submission, be allowed to frustrate the work of the Trial Chamber, the Office of the Prosecutor, and the Defence teams who are already involved in this trial, either wilfully by intransigence or sloth, and he could easily do that. A delay of three to four months, say, in his instructing counsel would mean that the question of joinder was not dealt with until virtually the end of the Prosecution case, by which time it may be pointless, and so I submit that the Trial Chamber ought to look to cure that defect at this stage. And the cure, I suggest, lies in the imposition of a back-stop order which requires a series of directions for the service of responses to the motion, which in his case ought to run from his instruction of counsel or by a certain date in any event, or time simply will slip away from us. And that's the submission I make, that in deciding how we come to resolve the motion, the Trial Chamber ought now to set time limits for General Tolimir that have certainty to them or time will simply slip away from us. As I say, it's difficult, he's not here, he doesn't have counsel, but in the interests of my client, that, I submit, would be an appropriate course now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I would just like to say briefly that - and Mr. McCloskey, I think can confirm this - I understand the frustration of Mr. Haynes and his position. However, I have it from good information that Mr. Tolimir has, in fact, requested a counsel who is not on the Rule 45 list and that counsel is in the process of obtaining an American co-counsel or lead counsel, excuse me, and perhaps - and I may be wrong about this - but there may be some hampering by the OLAD with allowing the requested attorney to even speak with him in a private situation without being monitored. I think Mr. McCloskey can verify that. I hope that would allay some of the fears of Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I support what my learned friend Mr. Haynes has just said. Could I correct something I said earlier? On the related topic that Madam Fauveau raised, she has pointed out to us and I think she is right that paragraph 36 actually suggests that time runs for all of us from the time that General Tolimir has obtained counsel. Therefore, the submission that I made earlier is redundant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Paragraph 36 says that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But Madam Fauveau wishes to depart from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I understand that. I take no opposition to that point. The point that -- the extension I was asking for, I didn't need to ask for in the first place and I'm grateful to her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It may be the morning. I don't fully understand what Mr. Haynes was saying. I know there are deadlines built into the system and I -- so I'm not -- I'm sure if I had a chance to talk with him I would get it more but I don't really understand what he was saying. I didn't fundamentally object to anything but I think before -- and I think he's already said this, we can't really set things for General Tolimir until he has a lawyer and the time frames that are built in are pretty good time frames. But I agree with him we do not want to allow anything to slip away but I trust the Chamber will not allow time to slip away and I don't think that will be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we are all in agreement that the longer this takes, the more convoluted the situation will become and the more difficult it will be for all of us actually to make valid or weighty submissions, and us to reach a reasoned decision, which is not circumscribed by supervening circumstances. So leaving this matter to be decided without any time limits basically would not pay us any dividends. But how to go about it, of course, I don't wish to comment arising from what Mr. Haynes has pointed out but obviously what he's suggesting is that if the situation of General Tolimir not being represented persists, then we should think about finding a solution. And a solution that he is suggesting, he's recommending, is to fix a time limit for General Tolimir to respond. I don't wish to comment any further on that because obviously it's a matter that at the moment we are not called upon to decide. I mean, it might arise if the situation persists, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I fundamentally agree with that. And decision in the discretion of the Court to respond to that situation absolutely. Now, Mr. President, the situation Mr. Meek has referred to is a situation I am aware of, and the area of finding counsel, choosing counsel and dealing with potential conflicts in counsel is something as you know that is normally handled at the first stage by OLAD. And many times the Trial Chamber comes in to review that decision and then, as we've seen, the Appellate Chamber can come in and review the Trial Chamber's decision. I think this will be, from what I know the situation is the first area of potential time taking. And it may be appropriate for the Trial Chamber to assist OLAD in that in some way but of course we will come to you or perhaps the lawyers involved in that will come to you, but I've gone through that before in the previous trial. It can be very lengthy and of course as you're aware in the Blagojevic case it went all the way to the final appeal judgement and was a very difficult issue. So it's an issue that's very important and has to be dealt with thoroughly, but we may be able to save time on it if the Trial Chamber deals with it initially. But it -- since you don't really -- it's not clear exactly what we are talking about, it will have to wait and bring you the details and -- when we get them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Any further submissions? There are none. I suggest we have a break now before -- and of course we'll come back to you with our first decision that would relate whether at least for the time being, for this week, we are going to proceed with these two witnesses or not, because I think that is the most urgent issue to -- that we have on our plate. So we'll have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a break of 30 minutes because we need to discuss a few things. Everyone is to be back here in 30 minutes' time unless we communicate to you a decision to resume later. But for the time being, I think 30 minutes, we think that 30 minutes will be enough. Yes, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I was just standing out of courtesy because I thought you were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me start from here: On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to express our gratitude for the way in which you presented or raised the various issues related to the joinder motion. This is how it should be in an open and transparent manner, and in a sense of cooperation. We appreciate that very much. We wish to communicate to you the following. First of all, we share completely your concern that this joinder motion is not one that should be allowed unlimited time to be decided. Rather, we are of the opinion that it needs to be decided at the earliest possible. This morning, in airing your views, you raised some issues which, in your minds, create problems or are of concern to you. We fully understand these concerns and we will be ourselves addressing the issues raised through the proper channels. For that purpose, we will need to stop again at 11.30, when we will be precisely embarking on this exercise, which I hope will bear fruit. And then of course we will come back to you later on, if there are developments. The third matter that I'd like to deal with and decide is there are witnesses waiting to testify. We have heard your submissions and we appreciate very much the arguments raised both in favour and against proceeding with the hearing of these witnesses. We have done a balancing exercise, and over all, in balance, we believe that we should proceed because we consider it to be in the best interests of justice at the moment. We decided to proceed with the hearing of witnesses until the end of this month. And then we reserve our position for afterwards, depending on what the developments will be in the meantime. So that is our position. We can start with the first witness, but we will need to stop at 11.30 and I don't know how long the meeting that we will have at 11.30 will last but, please, we ask you to remain at the disposal of the Trial Chamber in case we need to resume. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I just wish to take this opportunity to advise the Trial Chamber that further to consultations with the Prosecution during the break, and in light of the Prosecution's agreement not to call witness PW 108 for a minimum of 30 days, which as you know, Mr. President, comes close to the alternative remedy which was requested in our original motion concerning this witness, the Defence of Drago Nikolic will be withdrawing its motion for reconsideration of the Trial Chamber decision denying certification. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I'm pressing all the wrong buttons today. Yes. Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. So is the witness here? Yes. Okay. He does not have any protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Dragutinovic. Can you hear me? Are you receiving interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I told you good morning. Welcome to this Tribunal. You're about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, you're required to enter a solemn -- make a solemn declaration that you'll be testifying the truth. The text is being handed to you. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Dragutinovic. Please make yourself comfortable. Take a seat. Mr. Vanderpuye, whom you've met already, will be examining you in chief. He will then be followed by some or all of the Defence teams on cross-examination. Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel, gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long do you expect to examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do expect to examine him for about two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dragutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you to do a few things. One is to try to keep your voice up so the interpreters can hear you and also allow a short pause between the questions and answers, and if I put to you a question that's unclear in any way, please let me know and I can rephrase it in a way that you can better understand it. As a preliminary matter, would you just state your name and spell your last name for the record?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Miodrag Dragutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how old are you, Mr. Dragutinovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Kalesija municipality, in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And currently reside there or do you reside some place else?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I reside in Zvornik, Republika Srpska, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what your educational background is?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I am a surveyor, land surveyor, but I'm currently retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you received any prior military training?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: In terms of military training, I finished the school for reserve officers, that's a one-year course. Eight months out of it was training, and four months was internship or practice. I have no other military training.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us when that was and with what military force?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I finished the school for reserve officers of the JNA, in the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and later on, I followed certain courses and completed some training in those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us very briefly what you did prior to the outbreak of the war in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: You mean as a civilian? Or as a member of some JNA unit? I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. As a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I worked as a land surveyor in a construction company in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you part of any JNA unit between the time you completed your courses and the outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Like all able-bodied men, I was assigned to certain units of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what those units were and what your responsibilities were during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, I was an officer or chief of engineers in the Territorial Defence, and later on, when I was mobilised into combat units of the JNA, I was in a division-size unit in operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did there come a point when you were mobilised in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in 1991, not 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us the circumstances of that mobilisation and what your position was?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: There were some call-ups even before that, but in the events that were occurring in 1991, I was mobilised into a division-size unit in Bijeljina and I was one of the officers in operations of the command of that unit, of that division.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how long did you remain in that division?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: In 1991, I was there on two stints. In September, several days, and later on, from October 1991, until February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And in February 1992, did your position change?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I left for health reasons, but also my four-month stint of mobilisation was coming to an end, and I returned to the unit only in April in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, in August 1992, were you transferred to another location?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: In August 1992, on my own initiative, from a brigade that used to be part of that division, I returned to Zvornik with the approval of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what was your position when you returned to Zvornik in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I reported to the command of the brigade that existed at the time. I waited some 10 days to be assigned, before I was assigned to the brigade command, to the operations department, to the post of operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us what your responsibilities were as an operations officer?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I was an assistant, or, rather, an officer, and I had a superior who was deputy chief of operations and training. I worked on all the jobs involved in the department, and that included processing documents we received from the chief, that he had received from the Chief of Staff. Those were staff documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you remain in that position throughout the period of time that you'd been assigned to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: No. Later, I was assigned to be deputy Chief of Staff for operations and training, which was a promotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when did that occur?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: That was in December 1992 or maybe January 1993. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in your position as the deputy Chief of Staff or assistant Chief of Staff for operations and training, could you tell us what your responsibilities were?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: As assistant Chief of Staff for operations and training, I had my section and my assistants, with whom I worked on all the operative documents related to the Zvornik Brigade and all the documents related to combat training of units, and all the other documents that applied to the Zvornik Brigade and its units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As the deputy Chief of Staff for operations and training, to whom did you primarily communicate?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, I was supposed to communicate primarily with the Chief of Staff. However, in the circumstances that required the command to operate very quickly sometimes, I could communicate also directly with the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, were you required to submit reports concerning the operation of your section?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were these the reports that you submitted to the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I submitted reports to the Chief of Staff, and if the commander required me to, I could submit my reports directly to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in this particular position within the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember if there were any changes, but from 1993 until end 1995, or maybe mid-1996, until I was demobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just want to draw your attention to 1995, if I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge Kwon, I couldn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: His rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What was your rank at the time that were you deputy Chief of Staff of operations?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: For a while I was captain first class, before I was promoted into major.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What was your rank in 1995, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And at that time --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Reserve major, I have to emphasise that. Major in reserve because I was not an active duty officer. I was not a professional.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: During that period of time, who was the Chief of Staff of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: In 1995, it was Mr. Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And who at that time was the commander of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if you know, who was the chief of security for the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you describe for us, to the extent that you know, what was the personal relationship between Commander Pandurevic and Drago Nikolic during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: The relationships in the brigade in 1995 and the relationship between Pandurevic and Nikolic were okay, correct, fair, without any personal conflicts or any other conflicts for that matter that might have spilled over and involved either the brigade or their personal relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you describe what their professional relationship was during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Everything was within the framework of a successful functioning of a brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are you aware of any disagreements they had with respect to the operation of the function of the chief of security prior to 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: This could have been in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Right. Can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, in 1994, I can't recollect the exact date or month, Commander Pandurevic asked Mr. Nikolic to include into the regular combat reports that the brigade sent to the higher command also a report on the security organ. He wanted this to be a complete report that was supposed to be sent twice a day, but we did it once a day, and this should have been a collective report for all the organs of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was there a disagreement in terms of -- or to the extent that reports that were made by the chief of security were not incorporated in the reports of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Probably that's why Commander Pandurevic asked the chief of security to incorporate his report within our regular combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And to the extent that you know, was this issue ever resolved?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, and I should remember because after that I wrote interim combat reports that were partly dictated by the commander himself, in which the commander asked the corps command to resolve that issue. I know that he underlined that he was the brigade commander and that he wanted to be in command over all the brigade's segments, and that he expected the corps command to resolve that problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know if the corps command actually did resolve that problem?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how much time passed after that, but from the corps command we did receive an instruction about the work of the security organ and relationship between the security organ and the command that this organ belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And as best as you recall, what was the instruction that was received?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: To the extent I can remember, I understood this instruction as follows: The security organ had a certain level of independence with regard to all the other commands, let me put it that way, in the matters of all the duties and obligations of the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, you'd mentioned previously in one of your previous answers that the commander wanted to have control over all of the segments of the brigade, and I just wondered if you could just tell us briefly how the brigade was organised in 1995. We'll start with that. If you could just name the segments that you were referring to previously.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: The brigade command consisted of its staff, which had its organs and services, and it also had some of the subordinated units. Furthermore, the Chief of Staff had his assistants, the assistants had their desk clerks. That was one part of the command. The other part of the command consisted of assistant commanders. There was the assistant command for morale, religious issues and legal issues. There was the assistant commander for logistics. There was the assistant commander for security or the chief of security. The assistant commander for logistics also had his own services and on the strength of that segment was also a logistics battalion. In addition to the command, the brigade also had combat units starting with infantry battalion, mixed artillery division, a division for anti-aircraft defence, and I really don't know whether I have mentioned everything. I think I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. What about the engineering? Did it have an engineering --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: The engineers unit was a unit that was attached to the staff. The signals unit was also a staff unit. Also the military police unit was a unit affiliated with the staff. There was also a squad that provided logistics for the command itself. It was a very small unit, a logistical unit that was affiliated with the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And was there a personnel or reinforcement organ or unit within the staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: This was a service which existed within the staff itself, and it also had an assistant or the Chief of Staff for organisation and mobilisation duties. This is one of the services with the staff, similar to the services where I was affiliated with. There were other services as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Was there an intelligence organ within the staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Within the staff, there was also an intelligence and security organ headed by the assistant Chief of Staff for intelligence and he also had his own assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And was there a member -- the headquarters command, within the staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: The staff itself was an executive body headed by the Chief of Staff. It was the executive body of the command, and that body was headed by the Chief of Staff, and I was his deputy in a certain way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was there somebody who essentially took care of the administrative aspects of the staff or the staff office?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Within the staff itself, and within our -- my department, we had a staff office where we had a number of typists. We had a PC. That was operated by two soldiers. And we had some other office equipment that we used for that purpose -- for those purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was there somebody in the staff in charge of anti-aircraft rocket, rockets and defence?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Within the staff, all branches had their chiefs. We had a chief for anti-aircraft defence. We had the chief of engineers, the chief of artillery, and the chief of atomic and chemical defence, and we also had a chief of signals branch.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you say a chief of the signals branch, do you mean communications generally?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, generally, all communications that involved equipment, telecommunications, military equipment that was used for communication amongst the units and so on and so forth. But this was all within the brigade itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were these branches all attached to subordinate -- corresponding subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: They all had subordinate units, save for the chief of atomic, biological and chemical defence. In that aspect we didn't have a unit that would be in charge of anything because we did not have any equipment or means at our disposal to set up such a unit. There were some cases where we used means of protection against chemical and other agents but those were few and far between.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was there a distinction between the reporting of the assistant commanders and the reporting of the assistant chiefs of staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Assistant commanders reported directly to the commander, and the assistant chiefs of staff reported directly to the chief, but in essence, all reports are carried out in the same way. It only depended on who the reports went to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to clarify something for the record. In your answer at -- it says that the assistant commanders directly reported to the commander and the assistant chiefs of staff reported directly to the chief, and when you say the chief in that context, do you mean the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the subordinate units, to whom did they report?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: What units are you referring to? I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's fair. I'm sorry, I'll rephrase that. How about the battalions?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Battalion commanders reported directly to the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was there a subordinate unit -- a subordinate unit that was used for intervention purposes, special purposes?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: In the brigade, we had set up a manoeuvre unit which was independent. Its name was the Podrinje Detachment Special Forces. It was a manoeuvre unit for combat activities and it was also a mobile reserve of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And to whom did this unit report?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: The commander, the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the military police? To whom did they report?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: In order for the command to establish better communication with its units, the engineers detachment, the communications detachment, and the military police detachment were in direct contact with their respective chiefs most of the time. What happened most often was that the commanders of these units reported directly to their respective chiefs, which accelerated the whole procedure. We did not want to make this relationship any more complicated than it had to be, so there was direct reporting. And the same applied to the logistics battalion, which was a unit that was attached to the logistical part of the brigade. And it was just a matter of effectiveness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did it work that way also for the mixed artillery division and the chemical defence platoon and the reconnaissance platoons?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: The chief of artillery was also the commander of the mixed artillery division. So that he had a dual function and the same applied to other unit as well. For example, the chief of the anti-aircraft defence was for the most part linked with the division of the anti-aircraft defence and the division commander could report to him, but as a principle, these units and these commanders reported directly to the commander, the brigade commander himself. The battalion commanders, the division commanders, and commander of the Podrinje Detachment, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was it ever the case that the assistant commanders reported to the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: It could have happened, but not as a rule. There might have been legitimate reasons for that, if this was requested, if the Chief of Staff asked for certain data or information from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was this the structure and function of the brigade as it existed in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, that was the situation in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I could just draw your attention to a different area, I'd like to focus your attention on your movements particularly around the time -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I be heard? Okay. In the previous set of answers and questions, can I draw your attention to page 36 to 37, starting from line 25 of page 36? The military police reported to whom? And the witness answered that "What happened most often was that the commanders of these units reported directly to their respective chiefs which accelerated the whole procedure. We did not want to make this relationship any more complicated than it had to be so there was direct reporting." Could you clarify how that kind of reporting system could accelerate the whole procedure? In what sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you understand His Honour's question? And if you do, could you please explain that for the Court?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: If any one of these units had to be used in a -- in a task, then the commanders had to write to propose the use of these units to the chiefs. And then the Chief of Staff would issue concrete tasks to these units, the military police units, the engineers, the communications unit. At the same time, these tasks were also involving, for example, the chief of security if the task involved military police. In order to avoid duplication, if -- in that way the procedure was curtailed. What happened most often was that there was no time to apply the customary procedure that is normally used in the peacetime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What would be the normal procedure in normal time?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you explain what the procedure would be in normal peacetime?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: A certain task and the use of these units was supposed to be proposed by the respective chiefs to the commander and then the commander would issue his decision, that would be transmitted to the Chief of Staff. The Chief of Staff would then call the commander of these units and he would communicate the task to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So in practice --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I think we need to stop here. We will communicate -- we expect the meeting to last around about half an hour. So please make yourself available. If we anticipate or if we see that it's going to take longer, we will let you know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As we indicated to you earlier on, we've had some discussions through the normal channels, and we expect some developments following which we will issue further communications to you. At this stage, I can say we've done our part for the time being. Now, Mr. Vanderpuye, go ahead. We won't have a break now. We'll go right through to the end, quarter to 2.00. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Dragutinovic. I think just before we left off, I was referring your attention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Sorry for the interruption, Mr. Vanderpuye. But I couldn't follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Dragutinovic, I think just before the break, I was directing your attention to the period of time surrounding the fall of Srebrenica. First, do you remember when it was that Srebrenica fell, remember the date? No? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The witness seems to be indicating that he didn't receive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Check his channel because in my case it was switched off completely. Is it okay now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just before the break, I was directing your attention to the period of time surrounding the fall of Srebrenica. Do you remember what date it was that Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: 11th July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'd just like to direct your attention to the day before that. That would be the 10th of July 1995. Do you recall that day?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you did that day?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: On the 10th?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, sir, on the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to describe the whole day or a particular time period?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Why don't we start with the morning and we'll work our way forward.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: On the 10th July, 1995, the Tactical Group 1 that was part of the Zvornik Brigade and was under the command of Mr. Pandurevic, having received a task, a mission, from the superior command, was involved in combat and thus reached Zivkovo Hill and Rajna village, to the right side of Zeleni Jadar-Srebrenica Road. That morning, the forces of the 28th Division that were located in the Srebrenica area, and that is the BH army, mounted an attack against our units and the positions that we had reached early that morning, pushing our units back to the features of Biljeg and three nameless peaks that we called Three Teats, where we managed to stop and stop their attack. Later on, after Tactical Group 1 was involved, because, in fact, after introducing Combat Group 1, because the tactical group consisted of two combat groups, 1 and 2, so after Combat Group 1 was involved, we mounted an attack, pushed back the 28th Division, recovered the positions we had lost, and reached the line of Zivkovo Hill, Pusmulic village and Bojna village, and Bojna village is near the Zeleni Jadar-Srebrenica road, a little to the south of that road. That was sometime that afternoon, closer to the evening. In the area of Bojna village, we gathered the command of our unit and the Chief of Staff of the corps and the commander of this operation, General Krstic, arrived as well. That's where we were given missions for the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, the tactical group that were you a part of on that day, can you tell us when it was formed?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: It was established on the orders of the command of the Drina Corps on the 2nd or 3rd July, and it was ready for march already on the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter number 106, please, displayed in e-court? I'm told it's also 5DP 00106.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the document. That's the order from the command of the Drina Corps, and it says it was copied to the Zvornik Brigade as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And this is the -- this is the order that you've indicated from the superior command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's in fact the preparatory order ordering brigades to establish units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to see this order in your capacity as the assistant Chief of Staff for training and operations back in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, sir. Now, following the receipt of this order, was there a second order that was issued by the command of the Zvornik Brigade at the time, relative to the order we've just seen?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to this order, the commander ordered the Zvornik Brigade to prepare to establish the units specified in this order, and I wrote the preparatory order for the units of the Zvornik Brigade, which says emphatically that everything that needs to be set up for the unit must be established from the smallest details to the big things.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could I have 65 ter 318, please, displayed in e-court? Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the document. That's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And this is the document that you prepared in relation to the order that was issued by -- I'm sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: That is the preparatory order that was written on the basis of the Drina Corps order to establish units the size of a battalion from the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what were the components of this tactical group as it was set up?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: We can see it from this that this tactical group was made up of two combat groups, the first combat group being the Podrinje Detachment, and they were a standing unit. They were a manoeuvring unit and a reserve of the brigade. And the second was Combat Group 2 made up of two companies drawn from all battalions of the brigade. Then there was an armoured mechanised company, a combat firing platoon, and a logistical platoon. I think the command of this tactical group is also specified.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes if we could scroll down so the object 2.1 is on the top of the page as well?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you describe for us how the command structure of this tactical group was set up?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's written here that the commander is Lieutenant-Colonel Vinko Pandurevic and the deputy commander is the commander of the detachment, Milan Jolovic; assistant commander for logistics was Lazar Pejic; the operative officer was Major Dragutinovic. That is myself; chief of communications was Captain First Class Milisa Petrovic; officer for general affairs and procurement was Major Ljubisa Strbac; medical officer was Dr. Mile Bircakovic; the quartermaster officer was Dragan Jovic; then there was the -- then there was Sasa Maksimovic, also an officer. I'm not going to name all of them but that was almost all of it, that was the whole command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The order itself contains the entire command structure, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think there were any changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, back in July -- I should say, rather, on July 2nd, can you tell us what the purpose of this unit was? What was the established purpose of drawing together this tactical group?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: In order to form this unit, the superior command had to issue an order, and their order states the reasons why it should be established and why this order was issued. If I remember well, the main reason, the main purpose, was to separate the forces of the 28th Division between Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves and to reduce the enclaves themselves, that is to reduce the manoeuvring space for this 28th Division that had not been demilitarised after the enclave was turned into a protected area. It remained there as an armed force.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You indicated -- let me just take you back to July 10th, then. On July 10th, you mentioned that there was a second tactical group.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how did your group interact with that group? Was there coordinated action, for example?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: The mission of the Tactical Group 1 was on the Zeleni Jadar-Srebrenica road and Tactical Group 2 was to our left. It operated on an auxiliary axis. There was direct contact between our two units and there was also radio communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And during this period of time, did your unit maintain contact with the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you have the ability to communicate with the brigade from your position on the 10th of July?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: There was no direct communication. Our unit could only communicate internally, and with the forward command post of the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you maintain regular communication with the forward command post of the corps command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Communication existed, and it was used either on the request of the Chief of Staff of the corps or when the commander of the tactical group number 1 needed to communicate. That was Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And just for the record, where was the forward command post of the corps located?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Command post of the corps was in a place called Pribicevac. That's to the north-east of Srebrenica, sorry, south-east of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, if I could direct your attention to the 11th of July? Can you tell us what happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to an order from the corps Chief of Staff, Mr. Krstic, Tactical Group 1 from the Zvornik Brigade was preparing to continue its attack and enter Srebrenica on the axis of Bojna village, around the Zeleni Jadar-Srebrenica road.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you know when this order was issued?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was issued on the 10th, but missions were given to units on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And could you just describe for us what the circumstances were under which these mission assignments were given to the units? Did that occur at a meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: In Bojna village, where the tactical group had formed its command and gathered unit commanders, there were, if I remember correctly, also the commander of Tactical Group 2 and General Krstic. There were others, but I can't recall them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you recall who the commander of Tactical Group 2 was?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: That was the commander of the 2nd Romanija Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you recall his name?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I think his name was Trbic [phoen]. I think his name is Trbic still.
